terms.gloss: to end in (a letter or syllable)
terms.grammar: passive of terminō, with the ablative of the letter, or in + ablative or accusative
evidence: Quint. 1.5.62: genetīvō cāsū nōn e litterā, sed tis syllabā terminārentur (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 1.6.7: quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur
terms.comment: The letter goes in the ablative, with its name in apposition: in a litterā terminātur, it ends in the letter a (Traupman 238); cujus genetīvus singulāris in «ae» diphthongō terminātur (Traupman 222).

evidence: Quint. 1.5.61: nē in a quidem atque s litterās exīre temerē masculīna Graeca nōmina … patiēbantur
Quint. 1.6.8: dummodo per eandem litteram in īnfīnītō exeant
terms.comment: Literally “go out into”: the word runs out into its last letter. Neither Quintilian passage for this phrase is in Lewis & Short or the loci collections, and we have not been able to check them.

phrases.latin: omnia, quae e et o litterīs fatendī modō terminantur
phrases.english: all verbs that end in e and o in the indicative

phrases.latin: Prīma dēclīnātiō est nōminis, cujus genetīvus singulāris in «ae» diphthongō terminātur.
phrases.english: The first declension is of a noun whose genitive singular ends in the diphthong “ae”.

sources: Lewis & Short: termino · Lewis & Short: exeo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 222, p. 238, p. 246.
Quintilian passages not in Lewis & Short were read in the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
